source.title: MobileLLM: Optimizing Sub-billion Parameter Language Models for On-Device Use Cases
source.authors: Ze-Chun Liu; Changsheng Zhao; Forrest N. Iandola; Chen Lai; Yuandong Tian; Igor Fedorov; Yun-Yang Xiong; Er-Nie Chang; Yang-Yang Shi; Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi; Liangzhen Lai; Vikas Chandra

record.tranche_reason: The authors argue that scaling-law assumptions about architecture mattering negligibly need qualification for compact models, based on their depth-versus-width results. The results do not measure the specific loss, extrapolation, or compute-allocation outcomes in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports no held-out cross-entropy loss scaling, small-run loss extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its depth-versus-width experiments report downstream benchmark accuracy, not pretraining loss. Those outcomes are recorded as findings outside the listed versions; cited scaling-law results are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study argues against Kaplan et al.'s claim that shape matters little (V4). Its depth-versus-width sweep (19 models at about 125M and 350M parameters) reports only downstream zero-shot, TQA and RACE accuracy. It never reports held-out pretraining loss, so its results do not measure what V4 names. No result bears on loss scaling, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, other modalities or downstream predictability. The reader's T5 conflicts with its own 'discusses' relation; since no version is tested, T6 fits better. The architecture finding is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that for sub-billion models depth matters more than width. They also conclude that embedding sharing, grouped-query attention and immediate block-wise layer sharing improve weight use and accuracy. The resulting MobileLLM models beat prior sub-billion models on reasoning, QA, chat and API-calling tasks. They frame the depth result as contradicting Kaplan et al.'s scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: The study sweeps architecture depth and width and evaluates downstream benchmarks; it does not fit or test held-out-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Depth and width configurations vary; outcomes are reported across 125M- and 350M-scale model grids and multiple downstream benchmarks.

fits_no_version.finding: At about 125M parameters, average zero-shot accuracy ranges from 42.3 (6 layers) to 44.8 (24–30 layers). At about 350M it ranges from 47.1 (5 layers) to 49.8 (32 layers). Models under 10 layers do worst; between 10 and 66 layers differences are mostly about 1 point. There are no uncertainty estimates and one run per configuration.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For sub-billion language models at fixed parameter count, depth versus width changes downstream benchmark accuracy by a few points, favouring deeper, thinner models.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 235 (2024)
record.problems: The results relevant to architecture are downstream benchmark scores, not held-out pretraining loss. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the architecture sweep, and the token count used for that sweep is not stated in the reported table.
record.rows_left_out: The per-task scores for the Table 11 sweep and the TQA/RACE scores for the corresponding sweep in Table 12 are not included; the retained rows use the reported aggregate average for each architecture. Other architecture and weight-sharing ablations also report benchmark outcomes, but do not measure any listed loss-scaling version.

untested.parts: Loss as a power law in parameters, tokens or compute; no loss curves or fits are reported.
Extrapolation from small-run fits; none are made.
Compute-optimal parameter and token split; not studied.
Effect of depth and width on held-out loss at fixed parameter count; only downstream accuracy is reported.
Other modalities and training regimes; not studied.
Predictability of downstream scores from scale or loss; 125M, 350M and 600M–1.5B scores are reported but no scaling relation is fitted.
Fit or setup dependence of exponents; no fits are made.

record.verdict_notes: The authors' challenge to V4 rests on downstream accuracy, not loss. Even read loosely, the gaps between 10 and 66 layers are small (about 1 point); only very shallow models (under 10 layers) are clearly worse, which Kaplan et al. also observed. The extracted text has a garbled duplicate table near the start with slightly different numbers; the record's values follow Appendix Table 11, which appears authoritative.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs' loss from power-law fits on smaller runs.
The loss-minimising parameter/token allocation as compute changes.
The version concerns held-out loss; the study varies depth and width but reports downstream benchmark accuracy instead.
Other modalities and training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss; the reported task scores are not analyzed for such predictability.
Fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, fitting choices, and bending away from power laws.
